The shortfall is taken back on the rep's next statement as an Adjustment line with a negative amount, at the rate the original line earned. It is added once per change: a further refund adds only the extra difference, and if the refund is reversed or the invoice un-voided before that statement is created, nothing is deducted. If the adjustment is already on a statement and the refund is then reversed, the next statement gets a matching positive adjustment. An adjustment is not tied to the period you pick, and a statement can be created for an adjustment alone. Voiding a statement releases its adjustments along with its lines. Before you create a statement, the rep's card on the Earnings tab shows Includes $X in adjustments for refunds/voids since the last statement , and a Pending adjustments table lists each line. On the statement, adjustment lines carry an Adjustment badge and a link to the invoice, with negative amounts in red. If adjustments outweigh new earnings the statement total is negative and is labeled owed back ; it is an amount to carry against the rep's future pay. What it doesn't cover Rates are percentages only — there are no flat per-job amounts — and annual bonuses tied to company results (for example an NOI target) are not calculated here; track those in your accounting system. Reps can see their own statements; plans, rules and everyone else's earnings need the Commission permissions in Settings → Roles ( View and Manage ).
contracts-guide: Draft Just created. Nothing has been sent or agreed to yet — safe to edit freely. Sent The proposal went to the client. Also where a signed contract lands automatically if you edit its price, dates, or line items (see the callout below). Signed You (or the client) confirmed the terms. Sets signed_at and signed_by, and fires the “Contract Signed” automation/Zapier trigger. Active The contract is live and, if Auto Generate is on, eligible for automatic monthly invoicing. Expired Past its end date. The expiry-warning email/notification fires 3 days before this, for any signed or active, non-auto-renewing contract (cancelled, expired and draft contracts get no warning). A retry never posts a duplicate in-app notification. Cancelled Terminated before or at its end date. No further invoices generate. Weekly Bills every 7 days, counted from the contract’s start date. Billing Day of Month doesn’t apply. Biweekly Bills every 14 days, counted from the contract’s start date. Billing Day of Month doesn’t apply. Monthly The default and by far the most common — matches how most maintenance and package programs are sold; bills on the Billing Day of Month. Quarterly Bills every third month, counted from the contract’s start month, on the Billing Day of Month. Annual Bills once a year, in the contract’s start month, on the Billing Day of Month — e.g. a lump-sum snow contract. One-time Bills exactly once, on the first run on or after the start date; once any invoice exists on the contract it never bills again. Landscapt (CRM) Contracts Ongoing billing agreements — monthly amounts, seasonal overrides, sub-properties, and how signing and invoicing actually work. On this page What a contract is Status lifecycle & signing Billing mechanics Billing frequency options Ending or cancelling a contract Contract templates Worked example: multi-property commercial contract See also What a contract is A Contract (Landscapt → Accounting → Contracts) is the ongoing billing agreement behind recurring service — a monthly amount, a billing day of month, whether it bills a month ahead of service, and whether it renews automatically. It's separate from a Package , which defines the service cadence template, and from the Invoices the contract actually generates — see the See also section below. Each contract belongs to one client and is built from three pieces: Invoice line items — one or more entries pulled from the services catalog (or typed as a custom line) that set the wording on every invoice this contract generates. Both billing paths use it the same way: the lines become the invoice description, and the invoice's single line item is named after them (several lines are joined with commas). With no lines, the contract title is used. The wording is set once per contract and is the same on every invoice; only the amount can vary by month. A monthly amount grid — twelve fields, one per calendar month (January–December), each independently editable. "Auto Fill" copies January's amount into all twelve if you want a flat rate; otherwise leave months at $0 to skip billing entirely in that month. Billing settings — billing day of month, whether to bill a month in advance, payment type, PO number (copied onto every invoice the contract generates, so the client's accounts-payable team can match it), and two switches: Auto Generate (eligible for the automatic invoicing cron) and Active. A contract's end date can't be earlier than its start date — a save with reversed dates is rejected. Status lifecycle & signing Status is a dropdown on the contract itself — there is no e-signature integration behind it. Marking a contract "Signed" is a manual confirmation, not a document that gets sent out for a client to click and sign. Status What it means Changing a signed contract's terms flags it — billing keeps running. If you actually change the monthly amount, the monthly-amounts grid, the invoice line items, the start/end dates, the client, the billing day / frequency or the mid-cycle start setting on a contract that's already Signed or Active, the contract stays Signed/Active and the daily invoicing cron bills the new terms from then on. A "Changed since signed — needs client approval" banner appears on the contract until you click Client approved — clear flag (which re-stamps the signed date). The edit itself is recorded in the Audit Trail tab. Saving without changing any of those values — say, editing only the title, PO number or sales rep — doesn't flag anything. Because the signed-date is a tracked field, it's also one of the Zapier/automation triggers — "Contract Signed" fires the moment a contract's status is set to Signed, which is what makes contract signing a distinct, reportable event rather than just a status label. Billing mechanics Two paths create an invoice from a contract, and both use the same logic: Automatic, via a daily cron. Every contract that is Active, has Auto Generate on, and whose Billing Day of Month matches today (or the last day of the month, if the configured day is higher than the month has days) gets an invoice created. Manual, via the "Create Invoices" bulk action on the Contracts list — select one or more contracts and bill them right now, ignoring their configured billing day (but not the active/amount checks below). Both paths follow the same rules: The invoice amount comes from that calendar month's entry in the monthly-amounts grid; if a month was never explicitly set, it falls back to the contract's flat monthly amount. A month explicitly set to $0 is skipped — no invoice is created for it. Bill 1 Month in Advance shifts everything one calendar month forward: the invoice is dated and amount-matched to next month instead of the current one. This is what lets a contract invoice in, say, late June for July's service. Idempotency is enforced per contract, per calendar month — a contract already invoiced this month is skipped, so re-running the cron or clicking Create Invoices twice can never double-bill. Starting mid-cycle. Each contract has an If Start Is Mid-Cycle setting. Start on first full cycle (the default) simply begins at the next regular billing day. Prorate first period also bills the partial stretch from the start date to the day before that first billing day, as its own invoice: the period's amount × days in the stub ÷ days in the full cycle, rounded to the cent (a contract at $1,000 a month starting Oct 20 with billing day 1 bills $387.10 for Oct 20–31, then $1,000 from Nov 1). The invoice line names the stub period and shows the formula. It's generated once — by the cron or Create Invoices, whichever comes first — and applies to Monthly, Quarterly and Annual contracts (a contract starting exactly on a billing day has no stub, and weekly, biweekly and one-time contracts never prorate). A monthly contract that starts before its billing day (say Oct 20 with billing day 25) bills Oct 20–24 as the stub; quarterly and annual contracts starting before their billing day simply bill their first full cycle on that day. Turning proration on for a contract that has already started regular billing doesn't bill a stub after the fact. The stub uses the starting month's entry in the monthly-amounts grid when there is one, otherwise the flat amount. Why bill a month in advance? For recurring service, invoicing after the work is done means chasing payment on a moving target — the crew has already spent the labor and materials, and now collections is racing next month's visits. Billing a month ahead flips that: the client pays before the month's visits happen, so a late or disputed payment is caught before more service gets delivered on an unpaid account, not after. It's a cash-flow and collections-risk decision, not just a scheduling preference. A stop worked by two crews counts as one visit used against a contract's included visits. Both crews' hours still count toward the job's labor cost. Billing frequency options Every contract has a Billing Frequency, and both billing paths (the daily cron and Create Invoices) honor it. It's shown in Contract reports and as the Frequency column on the Invoices list. There is currently no field in the Contract dialog to set it; new contracts default to Monthly, and a different frequency is set through the API or MCP connector. If a billing day is missed (an outage, or the cron failing that morning), the contract is billed later in the same month rather than skipped — for Monthly, Quarterly and Annual contracts alike, as long as that period hasn't already been invoiced and the contract existed on its billing day. A contract whose client has been cancelled (or deleted) stops billing. Frequency When it makes sense The amount is per invoice, not per month. The contract's monthly amount (and each month in the monthly-amounts grid) is what gets charged every time the contract bills, at any frequency — it isn't annualized or divided. A quarterly contract worth $3,000 a quarter should store $3,000, and an annual $12,000 contract stores $12,000. Quarterly and annual contracts can't double-bill: a manual Create Invoices click mid-period bills that period and the cron then skips it. Bill 1 Month in Advance only applies to monthly, quarterly, and annual contracts. Ending or cancelling a contract While a contract is Signed/Active its jobs' visits are billed inside the contract price and don't auto-invoice. Once the contract is Cancelled, Expired, switched inactive or past its end date, completed visits on its linked jobs bill like normal per-visit work, on the client's usual invoicing frequency. When you cancel or end a contract that has linked jobs, the app tells you how many will now bill per visit before you confirm. Contract templates If you set up many contracts the same way — the same name, invoice description lines, monthly amounts and billing terms — save that setup as a template instead of retyping it. Save one. Fill in the Details tab the way you want it, then click Save as template at the top of the tab and give it a name. A template stores the contract name, invoice line items, default service, the twelve monthly amounts, billing day of month, bill-a-month-in-advance, payment type, auto-generate invoices, and include sub-properties. It does not store the client or the start and end dates. Use one. On a new contract, choose it from Start from a template… . The form fills in and you can change anything before saving. Editing and deleting. A contract keeps no link to the template it came from, so deleting a template (use Delete template after picking it) never changes existing contracts. Worked example: multi-property commercial contract A property management company owns 5 sites and wants one contract, one monthly invoice, and a summer-heavy price — full mowing season rate April–October, a reduced fall/winter rate the rest of the year. Add each of the 5 sites as a Property on the ONE client record first (More menu → Add Property, on the client's detail page — see the Clients guide, linked below). This is a single client billed as one account across multiple addresses, not several separate client records — if the sites actually need independent jobs, invoicing, or estimates instead of one shared bill, that's the parent/child client hierarchy (sub-accounts) instead, a different feature covered in the Clients guide. Create the contract against that client. In Contract Details, check Include Sub Properties by Default — this is on by default and documents that the contract covers every property on the client's account, not just one address. Set the invoice line items to the services covered across the sites (e.g. "Weekly Mowing — 5 Properties", "Spring Cleanup — 5 Properties"). In the monthly-amounts grid, enter the combined total for all 5 sites in each month — April through October at the full mowing-season rate, November through March at the reduced rate. There's no per-property line-item breakdown on the invoice itself; the grid holds one number per month, so that number needs to already be the sum across every site the contract covers. Set Billing Day of Month and, if the management company expects to be invoiced ahead of each month's service, turn on Bill 1 Month in Advance. Sub-properties is a billing-scope flag, not an auto-aggregation feature. Turning it on tells the contract it's meant to cover every property on the client's account instead of issuing a separate contract per site — but the monthly amount you enter is still one flat number per month. It won't sum up per-property pricing for you, so double-check the combined total by hand whenever a property is added to or removed from the client. See also Jobs & Packages — a package defines the recurring service cadence and visit counts; a contract defines the ongoing billing terms on top of it. Invoicing — what a contract actually produces: the draft invoices created by the cron or the manual "Create Invoices" action. Clients — adding properties to a client, and when to use the parent/child (sub-account) hierarchy instead.
crew-app-guide: Start Job You're on site and starting work. Your clock starts now, and the stop moves to In Progress on the office's dispatch board. Take a Break Lunch, or anything else that shouldn't be billed. The clock keeps running on screen but the paused minutes are subtracted at the end. Resume Back to work. Shown in place of Take a Break while you're on a break. Stop Job You're done here. Asks for optional completion notes, then marks everything at the stop Completed and works out the hours. The office reads the notes on the job's Visits tab and on the client's timeline. Skip One service at this stop isn't getting done today — no access, weather, client not ready. Asks for a reason, which the office sees. Landscapt (CRM) The Crew App What a crew sees on their phone — the day's stops, clocking on and off, breaks, photos, and sending work back to the office. On this page Signing in, and what a crew can see My Schedule — the day's stops Materials called for Drive time Start Day and End Day Working a stop When another crew is on your stop How your hours are worked out Notes and photos Suggesting work you spot What the office sees Signing in, and what a crew can see A crew signs in and lands on a home screen with three tiles: My Schedule , Dashboards , and Job Photos . That's the whole app for them — no clients list, no invoices, no estimates, and no sidebar full of office screens. Office staff in the field. An owner or office employee doesn't need a separate crew login. When their own login is attached to a crew (Team → Crews → Linked Login, or automatically by ticking Schedule Jobs Directly on their employee record), the regular home screen shows a My Schedule tile on any day that crew has a visit — or a stop still clocked in from an earlier day — and hides it on days with nothing assigned. It runs in the phone's browser, so there's nothing to download from an app store. It's also an installable web app: have crews use the browser's Add to Home Screen (iPhone Safari) or Install app (Android Chrome) option once, and it opens full-screen from a home-screen icon like a normal app; the icon opens the login screen, and a phone that is still signed in goes straight to its home. (If an icon was added before this changed and opens the marketing page instead, remove it and add it again.) It still needs a signal to load and save — installing doesn't add offline use. Inputs are sized so iPhones don't zoom in when a field is tapped, and controls are larger for gloved or one-handed use. If an action is queued without signal (clock in/out, pause, resume, drive start/end), it is recorded at the moment it was tapped, not when the phone reconnects — so a lunch pause that syncs hours later still subtracts the right minutes. Taps older than 48 hours, or from a clearly wrong phone clock, fall back to the sync time. The login belongs to the crew, not to a person. When you create a crew account under Settings → Users → Create Crew Account , Landscapt also creates a crew with the same team name and links the two. If you already have an unlinked crew with that name, the new login is attached to it instead of making a duplicate. You can change this any time under Team → Crews → Linked Login on that crew: pick a different login, or choose None to unlink. A login can only be attached to one crew — once it's used, it stops appearing in the list for the others. That attachment is what decides whose stops get shown, and the app refuses to clock in or out on a stop belonging to a different crew. A crew login that isn't attached to any crew (for example, one you unlinked, or created before this was automatic) signs in to an empty schedule. A regular user can be a crew's Linked Login too. If someone who works a crew has their own login (a crew lead or owner, say), pick their name in Linked Login instead of creating a separate shared crew login for them. They sign in as themselves, keep their normal access, and find the crew's stops under Scheduling → My Crew Schedule in Landscapt (the link only appears for someone linked to a crew). It's the same Crew App screen, with the same clock-in and stop rules. Being listed under Team Assignments is separate: that puts someone on the crew's roster for scheduling and costing, but doesn't give them the Crew App. Because the login is shared, the app records hours for the crew — see below. Individual people's times are handled by the office, not on the phone. Whether crews see prices is your choice: Hide pricing from crews under Landscapt Settings removes rates and amounts from everything they can reach. It's worth turning on if you'd rather the crew not be drawn into a pricing conversation on a driveway. My Schedule — the day's stops My Schedule is the day's work as a list of stops , in route order. Each card shows the client, the address, the services due there, and a status. A stop is a property visit, not a job. If a client has three services due at the same address on the same day, that's one stop with three services on it — the crew drives there once, so they clock in once. This is why the buttons say Start Job and Stop Job rather than per-service ones: the clock belongs to the visit to the property. Tapping a card opens the stop: the address (tap it for directions), the client's phone (tap to call), any notes the office left, the list of services, the buttons below, and — when the office called for specific materials on the job — a Materials called for card (see below). Materials called for When the office has planned specific products for a job (the Products section on the Job record, or on the dispatch board's job popup), the stop shows a Materials called for card listing each one with the quantity the office planned. This is separate from Request Materials below — it's not the crew asking for something, it's the crew confirming what was already ordered for them. For each material still pending, the crew can: Confirm or edit the quantity and tap Mark Used — the field starts pre-filled with the planned quantity, but the crew can correct it if less (or more) actually went down. The planned quantity itself is never overwritten, only what actually got used. Not Used — the material wasn't needed at this stop after all. Once resolved, the row becomes read-only and shows what was recorded. The web crew stop page (for crews working from a browser tab instead of the app) has the identical card and does the same thing against the same underlying job — either side works from the same planned list. Request Materials (in the native crew app) is the crew asking for something instead. Pick a stocked or project material from the catalog, enter a quantity and an optional note, and Submit Request creates a draft requisition tied to that job for the office to review. The quantity can be fractional, up to two decimals (half a yard of mulch is 0.5); maintenance parts aren't available in field requests. The crew never sees prices on the request. Drive time Drive time is tracked for the day , not per stop — it covers the yard to the first job and everything between. Tap Start Drive when the truck moves and End Drive when it stops. You don't have to remember to end it: starting a job automatically closes an open drive segment, so a crew that drives off and taps Start Job at the next property gets the drive recorded correctly without a second thought. You also can't start drive time while a job is running — stop the job first. Start Day and End Day The paid day runs shop to shop , not stop to stop. At the top of My Schedule the crew has a green Start Day button. One tap by whoever has the phone starts the day for everyone working on the crew that day; once it's running the card reads "Day started 7:02 AM — 3 on the clock" with an End Day button that clocks everyone out at once. If a job is still in progress the app asks you to confirm before ending the day. Who "everyone" is. The crew's roster for that date: the employees under Team → Crews → Team Assignments, adjusted by any same-day reassignment on the Crew Board, minus anyone marked not working and minus anyone whose Days on the Team Assignment don't include that weekday (an employee on one crew Mon–Wed and another Thu–Fri counts only on the crew they're scheduled with that day; a same-day reassignment always wins). Deactivated or terminated employees are never on a roster. A crew with nobody on its roster can't start a day — the button stays disabled until the office adds people. Forgot to tap Start Day? Starting the first job opens the day anyway, so payroll still has a shift. It's flagged Started at first job in the Payroll report, because the real start (at the shop) was earlier — the office can correct it there. Start Job and Stop Job clock the whole crew too. Start Job punches every working member in on that stop at the same moment and Stop Job punches them out. Those per-person job punches feed Job Costing; the Start Day / End Day shift feeds payroll. They are separate on purpose: drive time and shop time are paid but aren't on a job. The day is the company's day. Which calendar day a shift belongs to follows your organization's time zone, not the phone's. Started a job after End Day? Storm call-back, or End Day tapped by mistake: starting a job reopens that person's shift for the day, and the time between End Day and the new job start is taken off as an unpaid break, so the hours worked after End Day are paid and nothing is counted twice. Tapping Start Day on a day that has already ended does nothing; only starting a job reopens it. Working past midnight. A shift that started the evening before and is still running (storm work) stays one shift: after midnight the card still shows the day running with an End Day button, a second Start Day isn't offered, and the first job after midnight doesn't open an overlapping shift. End Day closes it once. A shift that has been left open for more than 16 hours is treated as forgotten: End Day doesn't close it at an absurd length, it stays open and the Payroll report flags it for the office to correct. Late, out, or leaving early: Edit Crew. Tap Edit Crew on My Schedule for the roster with each person's in/out time. For each person: Not working — out today (sick, vacation, hasn't shown). They are skipped by Start Day and Start Job, so they aren't clocked in by mistake. Clock In — arrived late. Their shift starts now, and if a job is in progress they join its punches from now. Left for the day — ends their shift and any open job punch, and marks them not working so the next Start Job doesn't clock them in again. Back — someone who left returns the same day. Their shift reopens and the time they were away is taken off as an unpaid break. If a job is still in progress, their earlier job punch reopens too with the time away taken off, so the hours they work on that job after returning are counted in job hours and Job Costing. Someone from another crew is helping today: Add someone to my crew today. At the bottom of Edit Crew, pick the person from the list and tap Add . The list shows people on the company's other crews who aren't already on yours today. They join your crew for today only (the same one-day move the dispatch board's Team Assignment makes), are clocked in like a late arrival, and join the running job's punches if a job is in progress. Tomorrow they are back on their usual crew. If they were already clocked in on a job with another crew, that job punch is closed at the moment you add them (their day shift keeps running), so their time is counted once — the same happens when the office moves them with Team Assignment on the dispatch board. The day clock is for the crew leader's login — the crew login (or the regular user linked to the crew), and only for that crew's own roster. Office staff fix anything after the fact in Report Center → Payroll (see the Report Center guide) or with Edit Job Times on the dispatch board. Working a stop Button What it does Start Job and Stop Job apply to the whole stop . Skip is the exception — it's per service, so a crew can skip the hedges and still complete the mow at the same property. A leftover visit on a job that is On Hold or Cancelled isn't on the crew's list, so Start Job and Stop Job skip it rather than starting, completing and invoicing work nobody asked for. A double tap, or a tap queued offline that replays later, is treated as already done instead of showing an error. If a crew already started the stop (Start Job clocked them in) and then skips it, their clocks stop at the skip — as long as no other service at the same stop is still running — so the hours still reach the Timesheet and Job Costing instead of staying open. If the stop has chemicals, a Confirm chemicals applied card lists each one at its planned amount. Enter how much was actually used, or tick Not used , then tap Confirm chemicals . When the company requires crew confirmation, Stop Job stays disabled until every chemical is confirmed. Chemicals on a service the crew skipped (or the office cancelled) aren't listed to mix or confirm and never hold up Stop Job. If the crew starts a stop the office never dispatched, its chemicals are loaded at Start Job so the card, the confirmation and the stock deduction still work. If the office left notes for the crew on the job, the stop asks the crew to Acknowledge them — and Start Job is disabled until they do . It's not just a record that the note was read, it's a hard gate: a crew can't clock in on a stop with an unread "gate code changed" or "dog in the back yard" note. If the office edits the note after it was already acknowledged, the gate reopens — acknowledging again is what re-enables Start Job. When another crew is on your stop If the office put a second crew on the same stop, your stop card says With <other crew> and the stop screen shows who else is on site. You each have your own stop: tap Start Job and Stop Job for your crew, and your hours are worked out from your clock times and your headcount only. Nothing you do clocks the other crew in or out. The visit is billed once by the office from the lead crew's stop, so your stop doesn't create its own invoice, and chemicals are confirmed on the lead crew's stop. How your hours are worked out When a crew taps Stop Job, the hours for that stop are: (clock out − clock in − break minutes) × number of crew members Those hours are then split across the services at the stop in proportion to their budgeted hours, so a stop with a two-hour cleanup and a half-hour mow doesn't credit them equally. That's what the office compares against budget on the dispatch board. Breaks come off the total. Pausing for lunch and resuming subtracts those minutes. If a crew clocks out while still on a break, the break is closed at that moment and still subtracted — nobody gets billed for a break somebody forgot to end. Forgot to clock in? If there's no clock-in on the stop, the app falls back to the job's scheduled start time and the time you tapped Stop Job. It's an estimate, not a measurement — clocking in is what makes the number real. Overnight shifts work. A clock-out time earlier in the day than the start time is treated as the next day rather than as negative hours, which matters for storm work that runs past midnight. That formula is the starting estimate. When people have actually been clocked in on the stop (Start Job punches the crew in), the visit's hours follow the real punches instead: each person's own clock-in to clock-out, minus their breaks, added together — so someone who arrived late or left early is counted for exactly the time they were there. The crew-size multiplication is used only when there are no punches for the stop. Once a visit is invoiced, its punches are locked for crew. After a visit's hours have been billed on a live (not voided or deleted) invoice, the crew app refuses changes or deletions to member punches on that visit and tells you to ask the office to correct the time. The office can still edit times. Hours on a stop are per crew , multiplied by headcount. Individual start and finish times for someone who came late or left early come from two places: the crew leader's Edit Crew button (see Start Day and End Day above), or the office in Edit Job Times on the dispatch board. Those per-person punches are what labour cost is calculated from. Pay is a different question: payroll uses the Start Day to End Day shift, not the on-job hours. Notes and photos Notes to Office sends a message back from the field. It shows on the dispatch board against that stop, so it's the right place for "couldn't reach the side bed, sprinkler running" rather than a text message to somebody's phone. If your connection drops and the app resends the note, it is saved once, not twice. Notes from the office. The job's crew note appears under Job Notes with its formatting (bold, bulleted and numbered lists), and you read and acknowledge it before clocking in. A note typed on a single visit is plain text. When the office adds or changes a visit note, your phone gets a "Note from Dispatch" notification only if that visit is dispatched, in progress, or scheduled within the next two days. A note on a visit further out is waiting on the stop when you get there, and you still have to acknowledge it before you can start. Add Photo takes a picture with the camera and attaches it to the visit. Before-and-afters, damage found on arrival, and anything a client might query later all belong here — they stay attached to the visit rather than living in someone's camera roll. Photos bigger than about 3 MB (typical for a recent phone camera) are shrunk on the phone before they upload (longest side 2,400 px, re-saved as a JPEG), so uploads don't fail on a weak connection; smaller photos go up untouched. If an upload fails you can pick the same photo again and retry. Suggesting work you spot Crews are at the property every week and notice things the office never sees. The Suggest work button on a stop sends that back: pick the service from a short list, add a note, take a photo, send. It arrives as a ticket for the office to price and quote. The photo is the part that matters most — with one, the office can usually quote the work without driving out to look at it. Crews never see or set a price here , and the list is one you control: tick Show in field upsells on a service under Services & Pricing, and give it a short prompt ("Overgrown or blocking a walkway?") so crews know what to look for. With no services ticked, the Suggest work button doesn't appear at all — that's how the feature is switched on and off. The full round trip — what the office sees, converting one into an estimate, and the two reports that show whether suggestions turn into money — is in the Tickets guide under "Field upsells from crews". What the office sees Everything a crew does lands on the Dispatch Board in real time: status moving to In Progress and Completed, actual hours against budgeted, notes, skip reasons, and photos. Nothing needs to be re-entered at the end of the day. The day clock lands in Report Center → Payroll (admins and managers only): each person's clock-in, clock-out, breaks and total hours per day, ready to correct and export for payroll. Dashboards are scoped separately. A crew only sees dashboards that have been explicitly marked visible to crews, so you can give them a job-count or hours board without exposing revenue. For the office's half of this — stop order, route optimisation, and exactly how actual hours are compared against budget — see the Dispatch Board guide.
damage-cases-guide: Case Type Required “Damage” or “Warranty” — a two-value select, defaults to Damage. Date of Incident Required Date picker. Find Client Optional Search-and-select that fills the name (and address, when blank) below — the case still stores the name as text, see the limitation below. Warranty Optional Warranty cases only — links the case to one of your active warranties, fills in the customer, and warns when the incident date is outside its coverage. See the Warranties guide. Customer / Property Name Required Free text, so a customer who isn’t a client can be typed directly. Property Address Optional Free-text. Description Required Textarea. Placeholder copy changes with the selected Case Type. Photos Optional New cases only. Take Photo opens the device camera; Choose Photos picks from the gallery (HEIC photos are converted automatically). They upload to the case right after it is created. Resolution Notes Edit only Only shown once a case exists — not on initial creation. Open Default status on every new case. In Progress Being worked — no system-enforced meaning beyond the label. Resolved Has a dedicated color in the shared StatusBadge palette (teal). Closed End state. Landscapt (CRM) Damage Cases Tracking property damage and warranty claims tied to a job — what a case captures, how cost rolls up, and a real current limitation in how it connects to a client record. On this page What a damage case is Where cases live Opening a case Reporting from the field Status Expenses & cost tracking Tickets Linking a Purchase Order Automations & Zapier The client-linking limitation What a damage case is A Damage Case is a standalone record for tracking either property damage caused during a job (e.g. a mower striking a client's sprinkler head or fence) or a warranty claim (e.g. a plant that died within its warranty period and needs replacement). Both share the same record shape — a caseType field of "damage" or "warranty" — so the feature is really one case-tracking model with two flavors, not two separate features. It is not attached to a vehicle-accident or fleet-incident workflow — there is no field for at-fault party, insurance carrier, or claim number anywhere in the schema. What it captures is closer to "an incident happened at a customer's property, here's what it cost to make right." Where cases live Damage Cases is a Landscapt tool, not a CMMS feature — it's listed in the crew-hidden Tools sidebar as "Track property damage & warranty". It lives at a single route, /tools/damage-cases ; the older /dashboard/damage-cases and /dashboards/damage-cases copies now redirect there. The page itself has two tabs: Cases (a searchable list — by customer, case #, description, or property address) and Reporting (a chart of year-to-date damage vs. warranty cost by month, with YTD summary tiles). Opening a case Cases are opened standalone, from the "Open Case" button on the list page — there is no "log damage" action hanging off a Job, Visit, or Ticket record that pre-fills a case. A crew member or office staffer fills out a plain form: Field Required? Notes A case number is assigned server-side via the next_damage_case_number() RPC. Creation retries up to three times on a unique-constraint collision (two concurrent submissions computing the same number), rather than surfacing a raw DB error. Worked example. A mower clips a client's sprinkler head while mowing a back yard. The crew lead (or office, once told) opens a new case: Case Type Damage , Date of Incident set to today, Customer / Property Name typed as "Sterling Storage" , Description "Mower struck and cracked a sprinkler head on the west lawn near the fence line." The crew lead snaps a photo of the cracked head on the form, and it lands on the case's Files tab (see below). The case is now visible in the list with status Open and $0.00 total cost until an expense is logged. Reporting from the field Crew and anyone with Job Photos access can also open a case without going near the Tools menu: Job Photos → Field → Damage Report is a phone-friendly form with the same fields (report type, date, customer / property, address, what happened). Submitting it opens a new case with the same case number, ticket and automation behavior as the form above. The field form also has the Find Client search and a Take Photo / Choose Photos control; if a photo fails to upload, the case is still created and the form says how many photos need to be added by the office. Employee injuries are tracked separately — see Injury & Near-Miss Cases . Status Status is a plain four-value field, changed from a dropdown on the case's status badge — any status can be selected from any other at any time; there is no enforced progression or guard rail in the UI or the mutation. Status Meaning Expenses & cost tracking A case's Total Cost is not a field you set directly — it's derived by summing every non-deleted row in damage_case_expenses for that case, both in the list view and the detail panel. Continuing the sprinkler-head example: the case's Expenses tab gets an entry — Date, an optional Vendor (picked from the shared Vendors table, or typed free-text if the vendor isn't in the system yet), a Description ("Replacement sprinkler head + labor"), and an Amount in dollars, stored as cents. The case detail panel's Total Cost updates immediately to match. Each expense row also carries a nullable purchaseOrderId , but the Add Expense form always submits it as null — there is no UI control to set it per-expense today. The only PO link that's actually wired up in the UI is the one at the case level, described next. Beyond expenses, each case has generic Files , Comments , and Audit Trail tabs shared with other record types across the app ( AttachmentsSection , CommentsSection , AuditTrailTab ). Files accepts images, PDFs, and common office documents. Photos added when the case was opened, or uploaded later, show as a thumbnail Photos strip at the top of the Files tab; click one to open it full size. Tickets Every new case automatically opens a ticket for the office to follow up on, whether it was created from the Open Case dialog or the crew's field form. The ticket is Open, normal priority, in the Damage / Warranty category, with the case number, customer, address, incident date and description in its body, and it is linked back to the case. If the customer name matches exactly one client, the ticket is attached to that client and appears on their activity timeline; otherwise it is created without a client. The case's Tickets tab lists every ticket linked to it (number, subject, status); click one to open it. You can link more tickets yourself: on the ticket, use Linked Records → Add Link , choose Damage Case , and pick the case. Linking a Purchase Order A case can be linked to a single existing Purchase Order via a searchable picker (by PO number or vendor) in the detail panel's header strip, and unlinked with one click. This writes to damage_cases.linkedPoId — it does not create a new PO or requisition from the case, and a case does not spawn a repair Work Order either. If parts or materials are needed to fix the damage, that PO has to already exist (or be created separately in Equipt's PO module) before it can be linked here. Automations & Zapier Creating a case fires a damage_case_created event, usable two ways: Landscapt's internal Automations — "Damage case was created" is a selectable trigger, filterable by Case Type. Zapier — listed as the "New Damage Case" trigger, delivered instantly like the rest of Landscapt's triggers. See the Zapier guide for connection details. The automation only fires if the customer name matches an existing client. Because customerName is free text (see below), case creation does an exact-match lookup against clients.display_name (trimmed, lowercased) purely to decide whether to fire the trigger — nothing is written back onto the case either way. If the typed name doesn't match a client exactly, the automation and Zapier trigger silently never fire for that case. A typo, an abbreviation, or a property name instead of the client's name on file is enough to break this. The client-linking limitation damage_cases.customer_name is a plain text column — there is no foreign key to clients.id . This is confirmed still true directly in the code, not just in CLAUDE.md's general note about informal client-name strings: the type definition has a customerName: string field and no clientId , the Find Client picker on the New Case form only copies the client's display name (and address) into the text fields, and case creation has to run an exact-match text lookup against the clients table after the fact just to fire automations — a workaround that only exists because there's no real relationship to query. Current impact. Damage Cases cannot be filtered or reported on by client the way Jobs, Estimates, or Invoices can — there's no client ID to join on. Two cases for the same client with slightly different typed names ("Sterling Storage" vs. "Sterling Storage LLC") show up as unrelated. And any automation or Zap keyed off a damage case reaching a client's activity timeline depends entirely on the typed name matching the client's display_name exactly. Per CLAUDE.md, migrating this to a real client_id FK is deferred until after the Landscapt dev/prod split — until then, treat the customer name field as a label, not a relationship.
dispatch-board-guide: Scheduled The default state for a newly created visit. Nothing has happened yet. Dispatched Sent to a crew — picked from the status menu, set by Dispatch Assigned, or automatically the first time you print or send a crew their day. Dispatching writes a “Visit dispatched” entry to the client's Activity timeline. In Progress The crew is on site. Picked from the status menu, or set automatically once a crew member clocks in on the crew app. Completed The visit is done. Picked from the status menu, or set automatically once a crew member clocks out. Skipped The crew did not perform this visit today, but it's expected to happen another time (weather, client not ready, access issue). Picked from the status menu or the visit detail sheet; you'll be asked for a reason, which is saved on the visit and logged on the client's Activity timeline. Cancelled The visit was called off entirely and won't be rescheduled as-is. Picked from the status menu or the visit detail sheet; asks for a reason the same way Skipped does. Hours: Man Shows hours as man-hours — a 3-person crew working two hours is 6. Hours: Crew Divides each visit's hours by its crew size, so the same visit reads as 2. Days All 7 days, Mon–Fri, or Mon–Sat. Your choice (and Hours) is remembered on this browser. Service, Date, City, Zip Identify the visit and where it is. Assigned Which crew (or Unassigned) currently owns the visit. Last Svc When this client was last serviced for this service — useful for spotting overdue recurring stops. A completed visit stamps its scheduled day, so a stop done on the 15th and marked complete on the 17th shows the 15th (a visit completed ahead of its scheduled day stamps today, and the date never moves backward). Start / End Scheduled arrival and departure window, editable inline. B Hrs Budgeted hours — from the job's linked service (production rate × team size), or the job-level total as a last resort. Shown to two decimals. Actual Hrs See the dedicated section below — this is the number that matters most for job costing. Shown to two decimals. Hr Variance Actual minus budgeted, colored red when over and green when under. Men Crew headcount used in the actual-hours fallback calculation. A value you set here is kept — editing the visit's times only fills Men in when it was blank. Qty, Rate, AMT Billing quantity, unit rate, and the job's value — the sum of the job's included service lines, the same figure the visit sheet and the client's Jobs card show. Notes/Icons Call-ahead flags, comments, and other at-a-glance indicators. Landscapt (CRM) The Dispatch Board The daily scheduling screen crews and dispatchers live in — visits, crews, status, and how actual hours get calculated. On this page Where it is Jobs vs. visits Visit status and the status menu Crews and assignment How actual hours are calculated Crew punches vs. visit hours Worked example Board columns Products (materials) on a visit Filters, search, and routing Bulk actions on selected visits Emailing or texting one client from a visit Stop order and Optimize Route Calendar view The Crew Board (shop TV) See also Where it is CRM → Scheduling → Dispatch Board. The board shows one day at a time — use the week strip at the top to jump between days. It's built for a dispatcher planning today's work and for reviewing what actually happened once crews are done. The board also works on a phone or tablet: below desktop width the toolbar scrolls sideways, the Client column stays pinned while you scroll the visit table, the side panel drops below the list, and buttons and checkboxes get larger tap targets. The Snow dispatch board is laid out the same way. The List / Calendar toggle at the top right switches between this daily table and a week-at-a-glance calendar ; the Crew Board button next to it opens the shop-TV crew assignment board . "Today" is the org's day, not the browser's. The default date is derived from your organization's configured timezone (Settings), so a dispatcher on the road in a different timezone still lands on the same day the crews are actually working — the same rule the Jobs list, daily load list, and job-costing reports use. Jobs vs. visits A Job is the overall piece of work for a client (recurring lawn care, a one-time cleanup, a snow contract, etc.). A visit is one specific scheduled occurrence of that job — a single trip out to a property on a single day. A recurring job produces many visits over time; the Dispatch Board only ever shows visits, one day's worth at a time. Jobs and visits track status independently. A job's status (Scheduled, In Progress, Completed, Cancelled, Skipped, Hold) describes the whole engagement; a visit's status (Scheduled, Dispatched, In Progress, Completed, Cancelled, Skipped) describes just that one day's stop. Completing today's visit doesn't complete the job if it's recurring. Visit status and the status menu Every visit row shows a status icon in the ST column. Clicking it opens a status menu listing Scheduled, Dispatched, In Progress, Completed, Cancelled, and Skipped, with the current status highlighted. Pick the one you want and the visit changes on the spot — a toast ("Visit marked Dispatched") confirms it. The same statuses are available from the dropdown in the visit's detail sheet. A single stray click on the icon no longer changes anything — it only opens the menu. That matters because moving a visit to Dispatched isn't just a label: it can fire "visit dispatched" automations and, as of now, writes to the client's Activity timeline, so it should always be a deliberate choice. Status Meaning Skipped vs. Cancelled. Skipped means "not today, but still expected" — the client still gets this service, just not on this occurrence (rain day, gate locked, crew ran out of daylight). Cancelled means the visit itself is off the books and won't happen as scheduled. They mean different things operationally, so pick deliberately — the menu shows both side by side. Both outcomes ask for a reason. Choosing Skipped or Cancelled — from the status menu, a bulk status change, or the visit sheet — opens a short prompt with Weather , Client requested delay , Crew unavailable , or Other (with a free-text note). The reason is saved on the visit, where it can be edited later from the visit sheet, and is written to the client's Activity timeline as "Visit skipped 9/9 — Weather" (or "Visit cancelled …"), so the office can answer "why didn't you come Tuesday?" from the client record without opening the board. Skipped and cancelled visits drop out of the day's numbers. The Totals row, each crew's stat card, and the Unassigned card exclude them from AMT and budgeted hours, so a day where three stops rained out shows what the crews actually had in front of them, not what was originally on the calendar. The visits themselves stay on the board (and under the Skipped / Cancelled status tabs) — only the rollups leave them out. Status also advances itself in a couple of places outside the board: dispatching a crew's day (or printing/sending it) can move visits to Dispatched, and a crew member clocking in or out on the crew app moves the visit to In Progress or Completed automatically. Crews and assignment The Team Assignment dialog groups visits into a column per crew, plus an Unassigned column for anything not yet assigned. The header for each crew column shows how many stops that crew has for the day. There are two ways to move a visit, and they do the same thing: Drag a visit card onto a crew's column to assign it, or back onto Unassigned to pull it off. Tap to place — tap a visit card to pick it up, then tap the crew column (or Unassigned) it should go to. The card you picked up is outlined, every column you can drop it on is highlighted, and a bar across the top of the dialog names what you're moving. Tap the card again, press Escape, or hit Cancel in that bar to put it back down. Unassigned cards also carry a shortcut button per crew ("→ Maintenance 1") that assigns in a single tap, and each assigned card has a ✕ in its corner that sends it straight back to Unassigned. Assigning to a person. On an employee's record (Team → Employees → Edit → User Settings), tick Schedule Jobs Directly and that person appears by name in every crew dropdown — new job, Edit Job, the visit panel and this board — and in Team Assignment as their own column. They get a one-person crew behind the scenes, so everything else (the crew app, payroll, job costing) works the same. Unticking it, or deactivating the employee, retires that crew without touching past jobs. If their login is linked to the employee and not already attached to another crew, it's attached to this one so they see the jobs in the crew app. A person who is already on a regular crew can't also sit on a second crew's standing roster on the same days; add them to their own crew for a given day with Team Assignment instead. Every crew change is recorded in the Audit tab as crew: Old crew → New crew ( Unassigned when a side was empty), with who made it and when. On a tablet, use tap-to-place. iPads and other touch devices don't support the kind of dragging this dialog uses, so a drag gesture will simply do nothing there. Tapping works everywhere — including with a mouse — so it's the reliable option if you dispatch from a tablet. A crew's headcount for a given day comes from its normal roster (set in crew settings), with same-day-only overrides layered on top from the same dialog — useful when someone is on loan to a different crew just for today. Move a person the same two ways: drag their name chip onto another crew, or tap the chip and then tap the crew they should work with. A member reassigned this way turns amber and is flagged as "on loan" for that date only, reverting to their usual crew automatically the next day; the ↩ on an amber chip sends them home immediately. People always belong to a crew, so Unassigned isn't a target for them. Within a crew, turning on Manual Route mode makes each visit row draggable so you can reorder the crew's stop sequence by hand (drag handle appears once the mode is on). It's off by default so that clicking into a Start/End time field to edit it doesn't accidentally register as a drag. Moving a visit to a different day — Move to Day , a drag on the board, or a bulk move — writes a "Visit moved 9/7 → 9/8" entry to the client's Activity timeline, so the client record shows when a stop was rescheduled without digging through the board's history. A visit the crew is working right now (clocked in, not yet out) can't be moved to another day — the move is refused until they clock out, because it would disappear from the crew's list mid-stop. Rows hidden by a filter are dropped from your selection, so bulk actions (Change Status, Re-assign Crew, Move to Day) only touch what you can see. Package visits have spacing rules. If the visit belongs to a Package job whose steps set a Min Days gap, a move that would put a step too close to its neighbour is refused with a message like "Step 2 must be at least 14 days after Step 1 (earliest 5/15)" and the visit stays put. See the Jobs & Packages guide. Two crews on one stop Some jobs need more than one crew on site the same day — a big cleanup, an install that takes a mowing crew and an enhancement crew. Open the visit, find Crews on this stop , and choose Add another crew… . (On the job page, use the same control inside the visit's Change date / crew editor.) The visit needs a crew already, and the stop must not have started yet. This is an office action: crew logins can't add or remove crews, and the Crew App has no equivalent. Behind the scenes each crew gets its own visit for the stop. That's why everything else just works: each crew has its own row in its own column on the board, its own stop in the Crew App, and clocks its own hours with its own men count. Rows for the added crew carry a purple Shared tag; the original visit is tagged Lead . Billing happens once. The lead visit carries the service's revenue and creates the invoice when it's completed. The added crew's visit shows $0, never invoices, and doesn't log a second "Visit completed" entry or fire automations a second time. The client portal shows the stop as a single visit. If the lead visit is skipped, cancelled or removed, the lead role (and billing) passes to another crew still on the stop; the lead can't be removed once another crew has completed its work. Labor is combined. Job Costing, the job's Hours and the labor reports add up every crew's hours and labor. The budgeted hours are split evenly between the crews so variance isn't charged the full budget twice. The day moves together. Rescheduling one crew's visit moves the other crews' visits that haven't started. A crew already clocked in stays put. Visit counts don't double. A shared stop uses one of a contract's included visits, and counts once toward materials spread across a job's visits. Chemicals are logged on the lead. The added crew doesn't get a chemical card, so amounts and inventory aren't counted twice. To take a crew back off, click the ✕ next to it in Crews on this stop — only before that crew has started. Removing the lead hands billing to the next crew. Each crew's order in its own route is set separately, and a change to the job's default crew doesn't overwrite a stop's crews. Snow visits can't take a second crew — they're staffed and billed per storm. How actual hours are calculated The Actual Hrs column is the real number used for job costing and crew productivity reporting — it is not always literally "time on site" unless a crew clocks in and out. The value comes from a fallback chain, checked in this order: An explicit override — if a dispatcher has manually typed a number into Actual Hrs for the visit, that value wins outright and nothing below is used. Real clock-in/out punches — if a crew member clocked in and out on the crew app for this visit, actual hours = (clock-out time − clock-in time − recorded break) × crew size. Scheduled Start/End time, as a fallback — if there's no clock data and no override, actual hours = (scheduled end time − scheduled start time − recorded break) × the number of crew members assigned to the visit. This is the formula used for the vast majority of everyday visits, since most crews don't punch in/out per stop. A scheduled End earlier than the Start is treated as running past midnight (End + 24 hours), so an overnight visit doesn't come out as zero or negative hours. Only worked visits count toward a job's Actual Hours. A visit that is still scheduled or dispatched can carry a planned Start/End on the board, but those planned hours are not added to the job's Actual Hours until the visit is in progress or completed. Reopening or cancelling a visit takes its hours back out. Break time is not billed or costed as worked time. Minutes recorded with the crew app's Pause button are subtracted from the measured duration before it is multiplied by crew size, so a one-hour lunch inside a nine-hour day with a three-person crew reports 24.00 hours, not 27.00. The deduction is applied identically on the board, in the job's rolled-up Actual Hours, and in every Report Center hours and job-costing figure. A break longer than the shift floors the visit at zero rather than going negative. An explicit override is left exactly as typed — it is assumed to already be the real worked figure. Editing a visit's Start or End time clears any stale override so the number recalculates from the new times rather than silently keeping a number measured against the old schedule. It does not touch the Men count: a headcount you've set on the visit is kept, and the times (or the crew's roster) only fill Men in when it was still blank. Hours are shown to two decimals everywhere on the board and in the visit sheet. Why the fallback matters. Without it, any visit a crew didn't clock in/out on would report zero actual hours — which would make job costing and crew productivity reports wildly understate labor cost on exactly the jobs where nobody bothered to punch a clock. Falling back to the scheduled duration × crew size gives every visit a reasonable, non-zero hours estimate by default, so reports stay usable even for crews that never touch the time clock. Clocking in/out with real times simply overrides that estimate with the truth once it's available. Crew punches vs. visit hours A stop keeps two separate records of time. Crew punches are one clock-in and clock-out per crew member, and they are what the Timesheet reports read. Visit hours are the visit's own Start/End, Actual Hrs and Men, and they are what Job Costing reads. The board keeps the two lined up wherever it can, and flags the stops where it can't. What stays in sync automatically Start and End. Changing Start or End on a board row, in the job panel's appointment fields, or in the visit sheet moves every crew member's punch to the same time and moves every service visit in the stop together. Correcting one person in Edit Job Times. If three people clocked in and out together and you change one of them because they arrived late or left early, the visit's hours become the sum of everyone's punch hours (each person's time minus their break, lunch and the stop's pause time). With several services in the stop, those hours are split across them in the proportions they already held. Labor cost is worked out from the same punches, so Job Costing and the Timesheet report show the same hours. For example, three people for 4 hours is 12 hours; if one leaves an hour early it is 11 on both. What changes the visit only Typing a number into Actual Hrs , or changing Men . Neither can be turned into per-person times, so the crew punches are left alone. Job Costing follows your number and the Timesheet report keeps showing the punches. If you are correcting a clocking mistake, use Edit Job Times instead so both agree. When you change a visit's hours this way on a visit the crew punched, its labor cost switches from the exact punch-based figure to hours × the crew's average labor rate , and the Job Costing tab says so next to Labor Cost. Editing the punches in Edit Job Times restores the exact figure. The mismatch warning. A small amber triangle appears in a row's icon column, and an amber banner appears at the top of the visit sheet, when a stop that has finished crew punches disagrees with its visit times or hours. Hover the triangle to see why. It appears when either of these is true: Start or End differs by more than 10 minutes from the crew's first punch in or last punch out . Visit hours differ from the total of the crew's punch hours by at least 1 hour and at least 15%. One person arriving late or leaving early does not trigger the warning on its own, because the first-in and last-out times are unchanged and a short shift is a small share of the total. A person who is a couple of hours short on a long job will trigger the hours check. That is the prompt to confirm the punches are right. The banner links straight to Edit Job Times. The warning only shows for the dates you are viewing on the board. Worked example A visit is scheduled 8:00 AM – 11:00 AM with a 3-person crew. Nobody clocks in or out, and no manual override is set. Fallback used Scheduled Start/End (no clock data) Calculation (11:00 AM − 8:00 AM) × 3 crew members = 3 hours × 3 = 9 man-hours Now suppose the same 3-person crew instead clocks in at 8:15 AM and clocks out at 10:45 AM — real punches exist, so tier 2 takes over and the scheduled window is ignored entirely: Fallback used Real clock-in/out punches Calculation (10:45 AM − 8:15 AM) × 3 crew members = 2.5 hours × 3 = 7.5 man-hours The clocked result (7.5) replaces the scheduled estimate (9) automatically — no manual intervention needed, and no override is written unless a dispatcher deliberately types one in. Board columns Which columns are visible is configurable per user via the column-visibility control on the board toolbar, and that choice is now remembered — it's saved to your profile, so it survives a reload instead of resetting to the default set every time. Column(s) What it shows Beyond that fixed set, the column-visibility control also offers a second, SA-style block of optional columns pulled from the client's and property's own records rather than the visit: Priority , Sales Rep , Notes to Crew , Gate/Lock Code , Turf Sq. Ft. , Mulch Bed Sq. Ft. , Gross Sq. Ft. , Linear Ft. of Perimeter , Linear Ft. of Edging , Yards of Mulch , and Parking Lot Sq. Ft. Any org custom field defined under Settings → Custom Client Fields shows up here too, as its own trailing column named after the field (with its unit in parentheses if it has one). These are all off by default — turn on only the ones your crews actually take off of. The same set is available on the Waiting List for consistency. The Totals row adds up what it can. Turning on Men, Qty, or any of the numeric extra/custom-field columns above makes the board's Totals row sum that column across the counted visits (see "Skipped and cancelled visits drop out of the day's numbers" above) instead of leaving the cell blank — so a Turf Sq. Ft. column shows the day's total square footage, not just each job's own number. Rate is the one exception: it's a per-unit price, so summing it across different jobs wouldn't mean anything, and that cell stays blank on purpose. Products (materials) on a visit Opening a visit's detail sheet from the board shows a Products section for materials tied to that job — the same editor used on the Job record's own Products tab, not a read-only summary. From here you can add a product, edit its quantity or unit price, and change its status (Used/Invoice, Used, do not Invoice, Not Used/Cancel, or reopen it to Pending) without leaving the board. "Used" and "Used, not billed" both take the material off the shelf — the difference is only whether it still reaches the client's invoice. Pick deliberately: a negative or blank quantity is rejected outright rather than silently rounded to something else, since the quantity on this row is what adjusts inventory once the status changes. Filters, search, and routing Status tabs — All, Scheduled, Dispatched, Completed, Cancelled, Skipped — filter the board down to visits in that state. Crew filter — a multi-select checklist to show only selected crews (plus "All Crews" to clear it). Search — a free-text box that matches client name, street address, city, zip, service name or code, crew code, and notes to crew. Click the × in the box (or press Escape) to clear it. The per-column filter's Crew option is a pick-list of your active crews plus Unassigned, so you choose a crew instead of typing its name or code. Map — the Map button next to Stats opens a map above the list with every stop in view, numbered in route order and coloured by crew; click a pin for the client, address, crew and status. It follows the filters and any new order or optimize result. Stops with no resolvable address are left off, and the panel says how many are missing. It uses the Google Maps key under Settings > Integrations. Weather — a chip in the count bar shows the National Weather Service forecast for the selected day (conditions, high/low, wind, chance of precipitation) plus any active weather alerts, positioned at the average location of the day's jobs. It covers the US and appears for days within about a week ahead. Date range — an optional end date lets the board span more than a single day when you need to look ahead. Stats and Call Ahead panels — Stats gives a quick summary overlay for the visits currently in view; Call Ahead surfaces visits flagged as needing a courtesy call to the client before arrival. Print Route Sheets — generates a printable, per-crew stop sheet (client, address, service, time, budgeted hours, and notes to the crew) for the selected day, including a separate sheet for anything still unassigned. There's no live map view on the board — routing is handled by the crew stop order, the Optimize Route action, and the printed route sheets. See the next section for how all three fit together. Bulk actions on selected visits Checking one or more visit rows reveals an Actions (n) button on the toolbar with a Change Status submenu, a Re-assign Crew submenu, and — separately — Email Selected Clients . Email Selected Clients opens a compose dialog addressed to the distinct clients behind the checked visits — selecting three visits for the same client only addresses that client once. It pulls each recipient's email from their client record and skips (with a reason shown in the dialog) anyone with no address on file or a hard email bounce; a Purpose toggle additionally decides whether clients marked Do Not Market are skipped (Marketing/promotional) or still included (Service notice — for messages about work they've already contracted, with no unsubscribe footer). Subject and body can be typed from scratch or started from a Documents email template (type "Client") — the same block-based template system used for invoice emails — and a row of merge tags can be inserted into the message at the cursor. Sending fires one email per recipient and logs to each client's Activity timeline. Completing visits in bulk (or one at a time from the status menu) also creates each visit's draft invoice. If an invoice can't be created, the visit still completes, and you see a warning — “N visits were completed but could not be invoiced” — instead of it passing silently. Mark those visits complete again to retry billing; it never double-bills a visit that already has an invoice. Change Status > Dispatched in bulk does what dispatching one visit does: each visit that wasn't already dispatched gets its dispatched time stamped (what the "visit dispatched" Zapier trigger and the crew app key on) and the service's chemicals are preloaded onto the crew's Chemical Mix card. Re-assign Crew in bulk sends each affected crew the same "New Job Assigned" push a single reassignment sends (for up to 40 visits per action, so a select-all doesn't flood phones). Completed visits are never re-assigned — a finished visit keeps the crew that did the work so its labor and history stay put; if everything you selected is completed you're told so instead. Sending selected visits back to the waiting list processes them one at a time, and the job's own date and crew only reset when its last visit goes back. Email Selected Clients requires the same permission as any other outbound client email (Email Activity's Send permission) — it isn't a separate, less-gated path to reach clients in bulk. Emailing or texting one client from a visit Open a visit and use the More visit actions (…) menu in the sheet header to reach that visit's client directly — the "we're running late" or "the crew is on the way" case. Send Email and Send Text open the same dialogs as the job screen's More menu and log to the client's Activity timeline. Each option only appears if you have the matching permission (Email Activity Send, or SMS Send) and is greyed out with "(no address)" or "(no number)" when the client record is missing one. Texting also requires the client to be marked Opted in to text messages ; without that, the dialog explains why and won't send. The same Send Email / Send Text actions are on a job's own screen, in its More menu alongside View Audit Trail, View Client and View Estimate. Replies to those emails go to the Reply-To Email set in Settings > Organization (emails still send from your company name on Landscapt's sending domain; with no Reply-To set, replies have nowhere to go). A one-to-one email you send yourself uses your own address as the reply-to instead. Stop order and Optimize Route Stop order is per crew . The # column numbers each crew's own stops from 1, so "#3" means that crew's third stop of the day, not the third row on the board. Reordering one crew never renumbers another. Drag rows in Manual Route mode, or use Reverse to flip the current order, or Group Stops to cluster each crew's stops by zip area. Either way the board shows an "Order changed — not yet saved" banner until you click Save Order . Reverse, Group Stops, and Optimize Route all work one crew at a time. Each tool groups the visits currently on screen by crew first, then reorders each crew's own stops independently — a mixed-crew day never interleaves one crew's stops with another's. Checking specific rows narrows any of the three tools to just those stops (a checked row a filter has since hidden falls back to the full board rather than an empty run); with nothing checked, all three act on every visit currently visible. The order is remembered for next week Saving an order does two things. It sets today's stop sequence, and it remembers that sequence for that crew on that weekday . The next time the same crew has work on the same weekday — next Monday, the Monday after — the board comes up already in that order instead of an unsorted crew grouping. You only have to route a recurring run once. The memory is keyed to the weekday, not just the crew. A crew's Monday run is usually a different neighbourhood from its Wednesday run, so each weekday keeps its own sequence. A job that moves to a different day has no remembered position on the new day and sorts to the bottom, which is your cue to place it. Jobs added to the route later — a new client on an established Monday run — also sort to the bottom until you drag them into place and save again. Saving the day always wins over the remembered order, so a one-off change for a single day never overwrites the usual route. Optimize Route Optimize Route reorders the stops currently in view by real driving time. The dropdown beside the button controls which way round the crew works the route: Direction What it does Nearest first Leaves the shop and takes the closest remaining stop each time. Usually the shortest total drive, but the crew can finish the day far from the yard. Furthest first Drives out to the far end of the route first and works back in, so the crew finishes near the yard at the end of the day. Optimize Route solves each crew's tour separately (in parallel) and anchors it at that crew's own starting address (set per crew under Team → Crews) — a mixed-crew day no longer needs to be filtered down to one crew first to get a real route. A crew with no starting address of its own starts from the Company Address in Settings > Organization instead. Only if neither is set is the route unanchored (routed by driving time without a shop to start or end at), and the confirmation toast says which crews that applies to. If one crew's route fails to solve (a bad address, a Distance Matrix error), the others still come back — it isn't all-or-nothing. After optimizing, each row shows the drive time to arrive at it: the first stop of a crew shows the leg from the shop (⌂), and every later stop shows the leg from the stop above it (↑). The leg back to the shop at the end of the day is in the banner, not on a row. The banner reports how many crews were routed and the combined driving time between stops and shop legs across all of them. An optimized order is a proposal like any manual drag — it isn't saved, and doesn't become the crew's remembered order, until you click Save Order . Optimize Route needs a Google Maps Platform API key, entered under Landscapt Settings → Integrations on the Google Maps card — see that card for exactly which Google APIs to enable (the same key also powers Nearby Waiting List and Aerial Measurement, so it needs more than just route optimization's own API). Type or paste the key and click Save Key — until you do, the card reads "Unsaved — click Save Key to connect" and the board can't use it. If the save comes back with "you don't have permission to change organization settings," your role lacks the settings permission and an admin needs to enter the key instead. Orgs on a plan that bundles Route Optimization, or that bought the add-on, don't need their own key at all — the platform's own key is used automatically. Calendar view Switch the toggle at the top right of the Dispatch Board from List to Calendar for a week at a glance: one row per crew, one column per day. The view and the week you're on are kept in the page address, so refreshing or sharing the link lands on the same week. Crew rows. Each row shows the crew name with its headcount, then its default roster underneath (the crew leader is marked). An Unassigned row appears whenever a visit that week has no crew. Cards. Each visit is a solid block in its crew's color showing the client and service, with budgeted hours at the bottom right. A recurring job carries a repeat icon and a completed visit carries a check mark. Budget bar. The bar inside each card is actual vs. budgeted hours , with the percentage printed on it: green while on budget, amber from 90%, red once over. It stays empty until hours are logged. Cells show their budgeted total, and a Totals row along the bottom adds up each day across every crew showing. Drag to reschedule or reassign. Drag a card onto another day, another crew, or both. The move saves immediately (and snaps back if it can't be saved). Completed, skipped, and cancelled visits can't be dragged. Drag and drop works with a mouse; on a touch tablet use the List view or the visit's own sheet to move a visit. Open a job. Click a card's name to open the job. The job page's Back button returns you to the same week in Calendar view (the same applies to View Job from a visit on the List view, which returns to that day). The filter bar above the grid narrows what you see: Crews (multi-select), Status (All, Open, Completed), a search box for client or service, Hours , and Days . Full screen fills the monitor, for a wall display. Setting What it does Each crew has its own color — set it under Team Settings → Team Details → Color (new crews get one automatically; the same color is used on the Crew Board). The roster under a crew name is its default roster (Team settings) — one-day changes made in Team Assignment or on the Crew Board show on the Crew Board, not on this grid. Creating a crew: go to Team → Crews → Add Team , enter a Description (the crew's name) and Color on Team Details (Team Code, Linked Login, starting address and Show In Calendar are optional), then click Create & Continue . On the Team Assignments tab, use Add Assignment to put employees on the crew's default roster. A Linked Login is only needed if the crew will use the Crew App — creating a crew account under Settings → Users makes the crew and the login together. Removing a crew from the board: go to Team → Crews and turn the crew's switch in the Active column off, then confirm. The crew moves to the Inactive tab and stops appearing as a crew to schedule on the Dispatch Board and Crew Board; its history is kept. Turn the switch back on (Inactive or All tab) to restore it. This is separate from the crew's login — deactivating the login in Settings → Users only blocks sign-in. The Crew Board (shop TV) CRM → Scheduling → Crew Board (or the Crew Board button on the Dispatch Board) is a Trello-style view of one day: a colored column per crew showing who's on the crew , what equipment is loaded on it , and which jobs it's running . It reads and writes the same data as the Dispatch Board, so the two never disagree. It needs the same permission as the Dispatch Board. Crew header. Headcount, jobs finished out of jobs scheduled, and actual hours / budgeted hours for the day. The bar is the share of the day's budgeted work that's completed; it turns red if finished work ran over its budget. Change crews by dragging. Drag a person to another crew (that move is for this day only and is tagged "today only" — dropping them back on their own crew clears it), or drag a job card to another crew to reassign it. Jobs with no crew sit in an Unassigned jobs column. Equipment. The Equipment yard on the left lists everything not on a crew today — trucks and vehicles first, then trailers, then other equipment, each with its photo if one is on file. Drag an item onto a crew to load it, or drag a loaded item back to the yard to unload it. Use the search box to find one quickly. What the crew needs. Equipment added to a job (see Jobs, Packages & Projects → Equipment to bring) rolls up per crew.
